setup.zh: 娘在油灯底下念那卷竹简，把行气铭十个字抄在账本最末一页：一个字一个格子，不许抢。心里数到一百二十，鼻子底下一根鹅毛，吐气的时候不许动。头一夜，你数到十二。
setup.en: By the oil lamp your mother reads the bamboo scroll and copies the ten characters of the jade inscription onto the last page of her ledger: one character to a square, no jumping ahead. Count to a hundred and twenty in your head, a goose feather under your nose that mustn't stir when you breathe out. The first night, you reach twelve.

recap.zh: 一冬：娘把行气铭十个字抄在账本末页，深、蓄、伸一个一个画上了圈；冬月廿二，马三身后跟着一个穿白的，嗓子又干又深，木牌烫了三下；刘豆芽拿一块桂花糕告了密；正月初五夜里，白衣人拿一面铜镜照你，爹坐在柴垛顶上压着嗓子说：「它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。」你把气沉下去，木牌凉了，镜子没亮。他把镜子留给了马三：「亮了，送信。」
recap.en: A winter: your mother copied the ten characters of the jade inscription onto her ledger's last page and circled *deep*, *store* and *stretch* one by one; on the twenty-second of the eleventh month a man in white came behind Ma San, his voice dry and deep, and the token burned three times; Liu Douya told on you for an osmanthus cake; on the night of the fifth of the first month the man in white turned a bronze mirror on you, and Father, sitting on top of the woodpile, said under his breath: "It's not your breathing it hears. It's your fear." You let the breath sink; the token went cold; the mirror stayed dark. He left the mirror with Ma San: "When it lights, send word."

zh: 雪地里，一个穿白的人，一面铜镜。
「它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。」
en: Top of the woodpile: one goose feather.
In the snow, a man in white, and a bronze mirror.
"It's not your breathing it hears. It's your fear."

story.zh:
那卷竹简，是九月十八夜里拿出来的。他等他爹的呼噜打到第三遍——他爹的呼噜是分遍的，打到第三遍，天塌下来也醒不了——才把竹简捧到灶间。他娘就着那盏黄豆大的油灯，手指一个字一个字地摸过去，摸到第一行，停住了。那一行是「吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新」。她道：「这一句……你外公念过。」

小满没见过外公。外公是镇上的穷塾师，死在他出生前头。他娘抬起头来：「这是……哪来的？」「山里捡的。」「……跟那条围脖一起捡的？」小满想起银月那句「你娘，用不着你说」，便道：「……嗯。」他娘便不再问了。

她从头往下念，念得很慢，后头的字，有一半她也不认得。念到「真人之息以踵，众人之息以喉」，她自己先愣了一愣：「喘气……喘到脚后跟？」小满想了一想，道：「那我是众人。」他娘道：「你是众人。」又念到一句「内气有一，吐气有六」，说吸只有一个门，吐倒有六个，她道：「进门一个，出门六个。跟咱家的钱一样。」

念到一片最老的，她念得格外慢。那一片没有几个字，一级一级排下去，像一架梯子：「行气：深则蓄，蓄则伸，伸则下，下则定，定则固，固则萌，萌则长，长则退，退则天。……顺则生，逆则死。」她拿指头一个字一个字地点：吸得深，才存得住；存满了，往外伸，往下走，沉到底，定住；定牢了，像种子一样发芽、长大；长满了，顺着原路退回来，一直退到头顶。末了那六个字，她又念了一遍：「顺则生，逆则死。」她抬起头来看他：「十个字，一个字一个格子。不许抢。」那天夜里，她把这十个字一个一个抄在了账本最末一页上。

小满急道：「那到底怎么练？」他娘是石坳村头一个会算账的人，碰上算不清的账，只有一个法子：「不知道值多少，就先数。」她把竹简摊到卷末前头那一片，指着一行道：「通篇只有这一句有数。」那一句说的是：「阴以心数至一百二十……以鸿毛著鼻口之上，吐炁而鸿毛不动为候也。」她道：「心里数到一百二十，拿一根鸿毛搁在鼻子底下，吐气的时候，毛不许动。」「鸿毛是什么毛？」「大雁的毛。」「大雁都飞南边去了。」他娘想了想：「先拿老周家的鹅凑合。」

小满掰着指头算了算，道：「一百二十……娘，人又不是鱼。」他娘没忍住，「扑哧」一声笑了出来。

便在这时，里屋他爹的呼噜，断了。不是打完一遍换一遍的那种断，是半截里「咯」的一声，断得干干净净。娘儿俩一齐转过头去，望着那道门帘。过了好一会儿，那呼噜才又响起来，响得格外卖力，一口气从头一遍直接跳到了第三遍。

小满看着他娘。他娘看着那盏灯，把灯芯掐短了一点，道：「念下一句。」

九月十九，子时。石坳村最冷的地方，是沈家屋后那座柴垛的顶上。沈小满盘腿坐在那里，鼻子底下横着一片削薄的竹篾，竹篾上粘着一根鹅毛。鹅毛是老周家那只大白鹅身上的，白天拔的，那鹅叫了半个村子，阿禾站在旁边，拿指头在脑门上点了一点：「鹅毛一根。鹅疼。利息另算。」

小满从鼻子里悄悄吸进一口气，吸满了，闭住，心里数：一，二，三……数要像他娘拨算盘珠子，一颗是一颗，不许赶。数到九，胸口发胀；数到十一，喉咙里像塞了一团棉絮；数到十二，那口气自己撞开了嘴，「噗」的一声，鹅毛从竹篾上飞了出去，在月光底下翻了三个跟头，落进了柴垛底下的鸡窝。鸡窝里一阵大乱。第二天一早，他娘的账上，「盐二两，十六文」底下，多了一行：

九月十九。子时。满，十二。毛飞，落鸡窝。

他这才觉出来，自己吸气，是拿嗓子「吞」的，一口吞进来，堵在胸口，胸口一鼓，肩膀一耸，数就断。他便试着不耸肩，让肚子去接那口气：肚子往外一鼓，那口气便顺顺当当地落了下去，比胸口深了一大截。头一个瞧出不同来的，是他娘。小满打小睡觉张着嘴，一呼一噜，跟他爹一个调门。十月初八一早，他娘的账上多了一行：

十月初八。满，夜里不打呼了。

他爹不服：「我还打呢。」他娘道：「你打。少了一个和声。」那天她在账本最末一页那个「深」字外头，画了一个圈。

到了冬月，他挑水从四担挑到了六担，上坡不喘，只好装喘，一面装，一面心里好笑。他娘在「蓄」字外头，又画了一个圈。
story.en:
The bamboo scroll came out on the night of the eighteenth of the ninth month. He waited until his father's snoring reached its third round — his father snored in rounds, and by the third the sky could fall and he wouldn't wake — then carried the scroll into the kitchen. By the light of the bean-sized oil lamp his mother felt her way along it character by character, and at the first line she stopped. The line read: "Puffing and blowing, breathing out and in, spitting out the old and taking in the new." She said, "This line… your grandfather used to recite it."

Xiaoman had never met his grandfather. He had been a poor schoolmaster in the town, and died before Xiaoman was born. His mother looked up. "Where did this… come from?" "Found it in the mountains." "…Found it along with that scarf?" Xiaoman remembered Yinyue saying *your mother doesn't need telling*, and said, "…Mm." His mother asked no more.

She read on from the start, very slowly; of the later characters she didn't know half. At "The true man breathes from his heels; the common man breathes from his throat," she stopped short herself. "Breathing… down to your heels?" Xiaoman thought a moment. "Then I'm a common man." His mother said, "You're a common man." Then she read a line that said there is one way of breathing in and six of breathing out — "Taking in the breath there is one; letting it out there are six" — and said, "One door in, six doors out. Like our money."

At one slip, the oldest, she read especially slowly. There were very few characters on it, set out step below step, like a ladder: "Moving the qi: deep, then it is stored; stored, then it stretches; stretched, then it goes down; down, then it settles; settled, then it is firm; firm, then it sprouts; sprouted, then it grows; grown, then it returns; returned, then it reaches heaven. … Follow it and live; go against it and die." She touched the characters one by one with her finger: breathe deep, and it can be stored; stored full, it stretches out, goes down, sinks to the bottom, settles; settled firm, it sprouts like a seed and grows; grown full, it goes back the way it came, all the way to the crown of the head. The last six characters she read again: "Follow it and live; go against it and die." She looked up at him. "Ten characters, one character to a square. No jumping ahead." That night she copied the ten characters one by one onto the last page of her ledger.

Xiaoman said impatiently, "So how do I actually practise?" His mother was the first person in Shi'ao Village who could keep accounts, and when she met an account she couldn't make out she had only one method: "If you don't know what it's worth, count it first." She unrolled the scroll to the slip before the end and pointed at a line. "This is the only line in the whole thing with a number in it." It said: "Count silently in the heart to a hundred and twenty… lay a swan's feather over the nose and mouth; when you breathe out and the feather does not stir, that is the sign." She said, "Count to a hundred and twenty in your head, put a swan feather under your nose, and when you breathe out it mustn't move." "What's a swan feather?" "A wild goose's feather." "The wild geese have all flown south." His mother thought. "Make do with the Zhous' goose for now."

Xiaoman counted on his fingers. "A hundred and twenty… Ma, people aren't fish." His mother couldn't help it; she burst out laughing.

Just then, in the inner room, his father's snoring stopped. Not the stop between one round and the next — a *click* halfway through, clean off. Mother and son turned their heads together toward the door-curtain. A good while later the snoring started up again, extra hard, jumping straight from the first round to the third.

Xiaoman looked at his mother. His mother looked at the lamp, pinched the wick a little shorter, and said, "Read the next line."

The nineteenth of the ninth month, the hour of the rat. The coldest place in Shi'ao Village was the top of the woodpile behind the Shens' house. Shen Xiaoman sat there cross-legged, a thin-shaved bamboo strip across under his nose, and on the strip, stuck fast, a goose feather. The feather was off the Zhous' big white goose, plucked that afternoon; the goose had squawked across half the village, and Ahe, standing by, had tapped her forehead: "One goose feather. The goose was hurt. Interest charged separately."

Xiaoman drew a breath quietly through his nose, filled up, held it, and counted in his head: one, two, three… Counting had to be like his mother flicking abacus beads — one bead is one bead, no hurrying. At nine his chest swelled; at eleven his throat felt stuffed with cotton; at twelve the breath burst his mouth open by itself — *puh* — and the feather flew off the strip, turned three somersaults in the moonlight, and landed in the henhouse at the foot of the pile. The henhouse erupted. Next morning in his mother's accounts, under "Salt, two ounces, sixteen coppers," there was a new line:

Ninth month, nineteenth. Hour of the rat. Man: twelve. Feather flew, landed in henhouse.

Only then did he notice that he breathed in by "swallowing" with his throat — one gulp, jammed in his chest, the chest heaving, the shoulders hunching, and the count broke. So he tried not hunching his shoulders, and let his belly take the breath: the belly pushed out, and the breath went smoothly down, a good deal deeper than the chest. The first to notice the difference was his mother. Ever since he was little Xiaoman had slept with his mouth open, snoring in the same key as his father. On the morning of the eighth of the tenth month, there was a new line in her accounts:

Tenth month, eighth. Man: no snoring at night.

His father wasn't having it. "I still snore." His mother said, "You do. One voice short of a duet." That day she drew a circle round the character *deep* on the last page of her ledger.

By the eleventh month he went from carrying four loads of water to six, and didn't pant on the slope — so he had to fake it, laughing to himself as he faked. His mother drew another circle, round *store*.

story.zh:
那一冬，他夜里坐在柴垛上，手脚不冷了。他娘起五更去井台淘米，两只手腕露在短了一截的袖子外头，冻得通红；他便把自己那件旧袄硬披在了她身上，自己穿一件单褂。他娘不肯，他说不冷，他娘只当他逞强，到底拗不过，披着去了。

冬月廿二，马三来收山风钱，一个人头五十文，挨家挨户地敲门框。马小宝跟在后头，身上穿着一件新的狐皮袄子，火红火红，毛领子一直围到下巴，把他那张圆脸托在当中，脑门上捂出了一层油汗。

这一回，马三身后还跟着一个人。

那人穿一身白，从头到脚，白得跟雪一个颜色，站在雪地里，倒像是雪自己立起来了一截。他不说话，也不进门，马三敲一家，他便在那家门口站一站，往屋里看一眼。他看的不是人，是梁上，墙上，炕头。看完了，再往下一家去。马三敲门框敲得比往年轻，走路也比往年慢，一面走，一面拿眼角往后瞟。

敲到沈家，他爹捧出一百五十文，那是他娘从过年的饺子钱里挪出来的。马小宝走到小满跟前，上下一打量：「沈小满，大冬天穿个褂子，冻傻了？」小满抱着胳膊，牙齿咯咯地打架：「冻、冻着呢，小宝哥。」马小宝拿那只捏着桂花糕的手，摸着领子上那圈狐狸毛：「看见没？真狐狸。八两银子。你家一年的租才二两，我这一件袄子，顶你家四年。」说着回头冲那穿白的嚷：「仙长！就是他！黑松岭里爬出来的就是他，脖子上还缠过一条白围脖，说是死狐狸皮！」

那白衣人转过脸来，看着小满。他的脸很白，白得没有年纪，看不出是三十还是六十。他开了口，嗓子又干又深：「围脖呢？」

小满胸口那块木牌，猛地一烫。

那嗓子他听过。在哪里听过，他一时想不起来，只觉得后脖颈子上的汗毛一根一根立了起来。他抱着胳膊，抖得更厉害了，道：「叫……叫我娘拆了，絮、絮了鞋。」

白衣人低头看了一眼他脚上那双露着脚趾头的草鞋，没有说话，又抬眼往屋里看。他看的是墙上那张缠着牛筋的旧弓，看了一会儿，道：「死的，不必看。」转身便走。马三赶紧跟上去，走出去好几步，才想起来自己的短棍还靠在沈家的门框上，又折回来拿，拿的时候，没敢看那张弓。

木牌又烫了一下，跟着是第三下，烫得他心口一缩。马家的人走远了，他把木牌掏出来，捧在手心里，小声道：「……你也看见了？那件袄子？」木牌慢慢凉下去，一明，一暗，又回到那个样子，像一个人在很深很深的地方睡觉。他只当她是恼那一圈狐狸毛。

小满一抬眼，看见他娘站在门里头，两只手拢在袖子里。他走过去，把她那两只手从袖子里拉出来，攥在自己手里。他娘的手冰凉，冰得他一激灵；他娘却比他还吃惊，手往回一缩，没缩动：「……你这手，怎么是热的？」小满道：「书上的第三个字。伸。」

他娘攥着那两只手，攥了很久，久到马三的短棍在别家门框上又敲过了两家。然后她把手抽了回去，道：「……进屋。」那天夜里，账本最末一页的「伸」字，也画上了圈。

冬月廿二。山风钱，一百五十文。满，手热。

腊月里，柴垛底下多了一双眼睛。那双眼睛是刘豆芽的。刘豆芽冬天夜里在沈家屋后下网捉麻雀，一只卖两文。他一连三夜，看见柴垛顶上冒白气——冒一口，停老半天，再冒一口，停得久得不像活人；还看见那人胸口有一块巴掌大的东西，在黑地里一明一暗。

腊月十几，打谷场上，孩子们在玩九头蛇。一个大些的孩子当蛇头，后头的一个揪着一个的后衣襟，揪成一串，每人一只手举在头顶，打头的「嘶」一声，后头的一个跟一个学。当蛇头的，正是刘豆芽。一串人一面跑，一面唱那首谁也不知道是谁编的老歌：

「一个头，吃一山，
两个头，吃两川，
三个头，吃三仓米，
四个头，吃四口田，
五个头，吃五谷种，
六个头，吃六畜圈，
七个头，吃七家灶，
八个头，吃八方烟，
九个头，吃九州——
吃完九州，还喊饿！」

唱到「七个头，吃七家灶」，歌声停了。马小宝穿着那件火红的狐皮袄子，嚼着桂花糕走了过来：「九头蛇？我也玩。我当蛇头。」刘豆芽慢慢放下胳膊，让开了。马小宝站过去，两只胳膊一张，「嘶」了一声。后头一个也没跟着学。那一串孩子，不知什么时候，已经散了，一个一个溜回自家门口，躲在娘身后探着脑袋看。马小宝一个人张着胳膊站在打谷场上，站了一会儿，骂了一句「没意思」，一脚踢飞了一块冻雪。门后头，不知哪个孩子小声唱了一句：「……吃完九州，还喊饿。」

老槐树底下，阿禾坐在树根上，往她那件旧袄的衬里一粒一粒地缝谷子。「禾种。」她头也不抬，「今年坡田又少收了两成，我挑了三十粒最饱的。」缝完了，她拿指头在脑门上一下一下地点：「一个头，一山；两个头，两川……九个头，吃了这么多东西。这账，得有人记着。」

小满正要笑，笑容僵在了脸上。打谷场那头，刘豆芽没走。马小宝从袖子里摸出一块桂花糕，递给了他。刘豆芽盯着那块糕看了半天，接过去，咬了一口，凑到马小宝耳朵边上，说了几句什么，一面说，一面拿手比了个巴掌大小，又朝沈家柴垛的方向，指了一指。

过了年，按村里过一个年长一岁的算法，小满十三了。

正月初四一早，他爹蹲在屋后的雪地里，看了半天。雪上一串小草鞋印子，从院墙外头绕进来，到柴垛底下便停；昨夜又多了七八双靴子印，绕着院墙走了一圈，在屋后站过，踩乱了一片。他爹站起来，拍了拍膝盖上的雪，只说了两个字：「踩点。」

正月初五夜里，小满没上柴垛。他把竹简塞进了炕洞，把木牌贴肉揣着，躺在炕上，睁着眼睛听外头。里屋他爹的呼噜，一遍一遍地打着。

子时前后，院墙外头亮起了火把。七八个，一晃一晃，打头的是那件火红的狐皮袄子，后头是马三。火把后头还有一个白影子，不打火把，走在雪地里，一点声息也没有。他们没进院门，从墙根绕到屋后，直奔柴垛。小满趴在窗缝上，一颗心跳到了嗓子眼：他爹的呼噜，不知什么时候停了。

火把围住了柴垛。柴垛顶上，坐着一个人，裹着那床破棉絮，一条腿直直地伸着，膝盖上缠着麻布，端端正正。是他爹。

马小宝举着火把，愣了半天：「……老瘸子？你在上头干什么？」他爹道：「膝盖疼，睡不着，出来问问天。」「沈小满呢？」「睡觉。」「那块夜里会亮的木头呢？」他爹老老实实地道：「在我儿子身上。」

那白影子开口了，还是那副又干又深的嗓子：「叫他出来。」

两个家丁踹开门，把小满从炕上拖了出来。他只穿一件单褂，光着脚，给推到雪地里，推到柴垛跟前。他娘跟着出来，站在门口，没有动，也没有说话，两只手攥在袖子里。

白衣人从袖子里取出一面铜镜，巴掌大，正面磨得雪亮。他把镜子一侧，火把的光落进镜子里，又从镜子里出来，变成了一团冷冷的白光，比火把淡，比月光冷，落在雪地上，像一只睁开的眼睛。

那团光，一寸一寸地挪。挪过雪地，挪过柴垛底下的鸡窝，挪过他爹伸着的那条腿。然后，朝小满挪了过来。

小满胸口那块木牌，热了。

不是烫，是热，一下一下的，跟着他的心跳。他的心跳得越急，那木牌便越热，热得像揣着一块刚出灶的炭。那光照到它身上会怎样，他不知道，也不敢知道。他想跑——打不过就跑，跑不丢人——可前后左右都是火把。他想憋住气，憋得越死，心口撞得越响，那木牌便越热。

那团光挪到了他的脚边。

头顶上，柴垛顶上，他爹忽然开了口。声音压得很低，像是自言自语，又像是在跟他那只膝盖说话，就跟在山里趴着、跟儿子咬耳朵的时候一个调门：

「蹲獐子，别憋。气往脚底下沉。」他停了一停，「它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。」

小满不憋了。他把那口气放下去，往下，再往下，沉过胸口，沉过肚子，像竹简上那句「真人之息以踵」，一直沉到脚后跟底下那片雪里。然后他把嘴唇收窄了，吐，细细地吐，吐得比一根头发还细，连自己的耳朵都听不见。心口那一下一下，慢了。又慢了。

那团光爬上了他的单褂，爬上了他的胸口，停在那里。

木牌凉了。凉得像一块冰，贴在他心口上，冰得他一激灵。那团光在他胸口停了好一会儿，又慢慢地挪开了，挪到墙根，挪进了夜里。镜子是灰的，什么也没亮。

白衣人把镜子收了。他没有走，就站在那里，看着小满。一个十三岁的孩子，只穿一件单褂，光着脚，站在正月的雪地里——不抖。

小满明白过来的时候，后背上的汗都冷了。他赶紧抖起来，抖得牙齿咯咯地响，抱着胳膊缩成一团。门口，他娘道：「孩子冻着呢。」

白衣人又看了他很久，久到马小宝手里的火把都烧短了一截。然后他转过身，把那面铜镜递给马三：「留着。亮了，送信。」

马三两只手接了，捧着，像捧着一块烧红的铁。

白衣人走了。他走过院子，走出院墙，走进雪地里。小满看着他的背影，看着他脚底下——雪地上，一个脚印也没有。

马小宝把火把往雪地里一戳：「沈小满藏着什么，我迟早翻出来。」带着人走了。

他爹从柴垛上慢慢地挪下来，膝盖「咯」的一声，落了地，扶着柴垛站了一会儿，一句话也没说，进屋去了。小满站在雪地里，脚冻得没了知觉，他才发觉，自己这一回，是真的在抖。

第二天，果然下了雪。隔了一夜，柴垛朝着路的那一面，高出了一截，一根一根码得严严实实，像一堵墙，从路上望过来，什么也看不见。风吹是吹不成这样的。

小满不辩。他在井台边上，当着一圈洗衣裳的婆娘，哆哆嗦嗦地道：「柴垛上那个，不是人。是个鬼，白衣裳，没有脚，坐着不喘气——鬼哪有喘气的。我娘夜夜给它上三炷香，它才不进屋。」这个鬼，去年交租那天吃的是饼；他娘说编得不好，鬼不吃饼，该吃香火——如今它改吃香火了。有人供着的鬼，马家惹不起，从此天一黑，马家的家丁宁肯绕半里地，也不从沈家屋后过。他娘听说了，当天夜里真在柴垛底下插了三炷香。账上记着：

正月初九。香三炷，六文。鬼。
story.en:
That winter, sitting on the woodpile at night, his hands and feet weren't cold. His mother went to the well at the fifth watch to wash the rice, her wrists sticking out of sleeves a hand too short, frozen red; so he forced his own old padded jacket onto her and wore an unlined shirt himself. She wouldn't have it; he said he wasn't cold; she thought he was showing off, but couldn't win, and went with it on.

On the twenty-second of the eleventh month Ma San came collecting mountain-wind money, fifty coppers a head, rapping door-frames house by house. Ma Xiaobao trailed behind him in a new fox-fur jacket, fiery red, the fur collar up to his chin, propping his round face in the middle of it, an oily sweat on his forehead.

This time there was someone else behind Ma San.

The man wore white from head to foot, white as the snow, so that standing in it he looked like a piece of the snow that had stood up. He didn't speak and didn't go in; at each house Ma San rapped, he stood a moment at the door and looked inside. He didn't look at people. He looked at the beams, the walls, the head of the kang. Then on to the next house. Ma San rapped more softly than in other years, walked more slowly, and kept glancing back out of the corner of his eye.

At the Shens', his father held out a hundred and fifty coppers — money his mother had taken from what was saved for the New Year dumplings. Ma Xiaobao came up to Xiaoman and looked him up and down. "Shen Xiaoman, a shirt in the middle of winter — frozen stupid?" Xiaoman hugged himself, teeth chattering. "Fr-freezing, Xiaobao-ge." Ma Xiaobao stroked the ring of fox fur at his collar with the hand that held an osmanthus cake. "See this? Real fox. Eight taels of silver. Your family's whole year's rent is two taels; this one jacket's worth four years of you." Then he turned and shouted to the man in white: "Immortal sir! That's him! He's the one who crawled out of Black Pine Ridge — he had a white scarf round his neck, said it was a dead fox's pelt!"

The man in white turned his face and looked at Xiaoman. His face was very white, white beyond any age; there was no telling if he was thirty or sixty. When he spoke, his voice was dry and deep: "Where's the scarf?"

The token at Xiaoman's chest flared hot.

He had heard that voice. Where, he couldn't think; he only felt the hairs on the back of his neck rise one by one. He hugged himself and shook harder: "M-my mother unpicked it, st-stuffed our shoes with it."

The man in white glanced down at the straw sandals with his toes poking out of them, said nothing, and looked into the house again. What he looked at was the old bow on the wall, wound with ox sinew; he looked at it a while, and said, "A dead one — no need to look." He turned and went. Ma San hurried after him, got several paces before he remembered his club was still leaning on the Shens' door-frame, and came back for it; as he took it, he didn't dare look at the bow.

The token burned again, and then a third time, so hot his heart shrank. When the Mas had gone off, he took the token out and cupped it in his palm and said under his breath, "…You saw it too? That jacket?" Slowly the token cooled — bright, then dim — back to how it was, like someone sleeping very, very deep. He took it she was cross about the ring of fox fur.

Xiaoman looked up and saw his mother standing inside the door, hands tucked in her sleeves. He went over, drew her two hands out of the sleeves, and held them in his. Her hands were ice-cold, so cold he started; but she was more startled than he was, and tried to pull them back, and couldn't: "…Why are your hands warm?" Xiaoman said, "The third word in the book. *Stretch*."

His mother held his two hands a long time, so long that Ma San's club rapped two more door-frames down the lane. Then she drew her hands back and said, "…Inside." That night the character *stretch* on the last page of the ledger got its circle too.

Eleventh month, twenty-second. Mountain-wind money, a hundred and fifty coppers. Man: warm hands.

In the twelfth month there was a pair of eyes at the foot of the woodpile. The eyes were Liu Douya's. On winter nights Liu Douya set nets behind the Shens' house for sparrows, two coppers apiece. Three nights running he saw white breath rising from the top of the woodpile — one puff, a long, long stop, another puff, stopping so long it didn't seem like a living person; and he saw on the person's chest a thing the size of a palm, glowing and dimming in the dark.

Some day in the middle of the twelfth month, on the threshing floor, the children were playing Nine-Headed Snake. A bigger child was the head; behind him the rest each held the back of the jacket in front, one long string, each with a hand raised over their head; the head hissed, and the rest hissed after him one by one. The head was Liu Douya. As the string ran it sang the old song nobody knew who'd made:

"One head eats one mountain,
Two heads eat two rivers,
Three heads eat three granaries,
Four heads eat four fields,
Five heads eat the five grains' seed,
Six heads eat six pens of beasts,
Seven heads eat seven family stoves,
Eight heads eat eight directions' smoke,
Nine heads eat the Nine Provinces —
Ate the Nine Provinces, still cries hungry!"

At "Seven heads eat seven family stoves" the singing stopped. Ma Xiaobao came over in his fiery fox-fur jacket, chewing an osmanthus cake. "Nine-Headed Snake? I'll play. I'll be the head." Liu Douya slowly lowered his arm and stepped aside. Ma Xiaobao took his place, spread both arms, and hissed. Nobody behind him hissed back. The string of children had broken up at some point, slipping back one by one to their own doorways, peeping out from behind their mothers. Ma Xiaobao stood alone on the threshing floor with his arms spread, stood a while, swore "Boring," and kicked a clod of frozen snow. From behind some door a child sang under its breath: "…Ate the Nine Provinces, still cries hungry."

Under the old locust tree Ahe sat on a root, sewing grains of rice one by one into the lining of her old jacket. "Seed rice," she said without looking up. "The slope fields came in two-tenths short again this year. I picked the thirty fullest." When she'd finished she tapped her forehead, again and again: "One head, one mountain; two heads, two rivers… Nine heads ate all that. Somebody has to keep that account."

Xiaoman was about to laugh, and the laugh froze on his face. Across the threshing floor, Liu Douya hadn't gone. Ma Xiaobao took an osmanthus cake from his sleeve and held it out to him. Liu Douya stared at the cake a long time, took it, bit it, and leaned to Ma Xiaobao's ear and said something; as he spoke he made a shape the size of a palm with his hand, and then pointed toward the Shens' woodpile.

With the new year — by the village way of counting, a year older at each New Year — Xiaoman was thirteen.

Early on the fourth of the first month his father crouched in the snow behind the house and looked for a long time. In the snow a line of small straw-sandal prints came round in from outside the yard wall and stopped at the foot of the woodpile; and last night there had been seven or eight pairs of boot prints besides, round the wall and back, standing behind the house, trampling a patch flat. His father stood up, brushed the snow off his knee, and said only two words: "Scouting us."

On the night of the fifth of the first month Xiaoman didn't go up the woodpile. He pushed the bamboo scroll into the flue of the kang, kept the token against his skin, and lay on the kang with his eyes open, listening outside. In the inner room his father's snoring went on round after round.

Around the hour of the rat, torches lit up beyond the yard wall. Seven or eight of them, swaying; at the front the fiery fox-fur jacket, behind it Ma San. Behind the torches came a white shape that carried no torch and walked over the snow without a sound. They didn't come in at the gate; they went round along the wall to the back of the house, straight for the woodpile. Xiaoman lay with his eye to the crack of the window, his heart in his throat: at some point his father's snoring had stopped.

The torches ringed the woodpile. On top of the woodpile sat a man wrapped in that ragged quilt, one leg stretched straight out, the knee bound in hemp, sitting square. It was his father.

Ma Xiaobao held up his torch and gaped a long while. "…Old Cripple? What are you doing up there?" His father said, "Knee hurts, can't sleep. Came out to ask the sky." "Where's Shen Xiaoman?" "Asleep." "And that bit of wood that glows at night?" His father said, quite honestly, "On my son."

The white shape spoke — that same dry, deep voice: "Bring him out."

Two men kicked the door open and dragged Xiaoman off the kang. He had on only an unlined shirt and no shoes; they pushed him out into the snow, up to the foot of the woodpile. His mother came out after him and stood in the doorway, not moving, not speaking, her two hands clenched in her sleeves.

The man in white took a bronze mirror from his sleeve, the size of a palm, its face polished bright as snow. He tilted it; the torchlight fell into the mirror and came out of it again as a cold patch of white light, paler than the torches, colder than the moon, lying on the snow like an open eye.

The light moved, inch by inch. Over the snow, over the henhouse at the foot of the pile, over his father's outstretched leg. Then it moved toward Xiaoman.

The token at Xiaoman's chest grew warm.

Not burning — warm, beat after beat, keeping time with his heart. The faster his heart went, the warmer it grew, until it was like carrying a coal fresh out of the stove. What would happen when the light reached it, he didn't know, and didn't dare know. He wanted to run — if you can't win, run; running's no shame — but there were torches front, back and both sides. He wanted to hold his breath, and the harder he held it, the louder his heart knocked, and the warmer the token grew.

The light reached his feet.

Overhead, on top of the woodpile, his father spoke. His voice was very low, as if talking to himself, or to that knee of his — the same pitch he used lying out in the hills, whispering in his son's ear:

"Stalking a river deer, don't hold it in. Let the breath sink to your feet." He paused. "It's not your breathing it hears. It's your fear."

Xiaoman stopped holding it. He let the breath go down, and further down, past the chest, past the belly, like that line in the scroll — *the true man breathes from his heels* — all the way down into the snow under his heels. Then he narrowed his lips and breathed out, fine and thin, thinner than a hair, so his own ears couldn't hear it. The knocking at his heart slowed. Slowed again.

The light climbed his shirt, climbed to his chest, and stopped there.

The token went cold. Cold as ice against his heart, so cold he flinched. The light rested on his chest a good while, then slowly moved off, to the foot of the wall, and away into the night. The mirror was grey. Nothing had lit.

The man in white put the mirror away. He didn't leave; he stood there looking at Xiaoman. A boy of thirteen in an unlined shirt, barefoot, standing in the snow of the first month — not shivering.

By the time Xiaoman understood, the sweat on his back had gone cold. He started shivering at once, teeth chattering, hugging himself into a ball. In the doorway his mother said, "The child's freezing."

The man in white looked at him a long time again, till the torch in Ma Xiaobao's hand had burned down a good length. Then he turned and handed the bronze mirror to Ma San: "Keep it. When it lights, send word."

Ma San took it in both hands and held it like a piece of red-hot iron.

The man in white left. He walked across the yard, out past the wall, away over the snow. Xiaoman watched his back, watched the ground under his feet — in the snow, not one footprint.

Ma Xiaobao stabbed his torch into the snow. "Whatever Shen Xiaoman's hiding, I'll dig it out sooner or later," and led his men away.

His father eased himself down from the woodpile; his knee went *clack* as he landed, and he stood holding the pile a while, said not a word, and went inside. Xiaoman stood in the snow till his feet had no feeling left before he noticed that this time he really was shivering.

The next day, sure enough, it snowed. A night later the side of the woodpile facing the road had grown taller, log fitted on log, tight as a wall; from the road you couldn't see a thing. No wind stacks wood like that.

Xiaoman didn't argue it. At the well, in front of a ring of women doing their washing, he said, shivering: "That thing on the woodpile isn't a person. It's a ghost — white clothes, no feet, sits there and doesn't breathe — when did a ghost ever breathe? My ma lights it three sticks of incense every night, and that's why it doesn't come in." The same ghost, on the day the rent was paid last autumn, had eaten flatbread; his mother had said that was badly made up, ghosts don't eat bread, they eat incense — and now it ate incense. A ghost that somebody keeps fed, the Mas couldn't afford to cross; from then on, once it got dark the Ma servants would rather go half a li round than pass behind the Shens' house. When his mother heard, that very night she really did stick three sticks of incense at the foot of the woodpile. In the accounts:

First month, ninth. Incense, three sticks, six coppers. Ghost.
